6970:
Goings-on means activities, events, or things that are happening — especially ones that seem strange, suspicious, morally questionable, or at least worth talking about.

Think of it as someone watching a situation and noting down everything that's taking place — usually with a sense of curiosity, amusement, or mild disapproval.

This is the most important thing to understand: goings-on is rarely neutral. It almost always carries one of these flavours:

  • Suspicion — something seems off here
  • Disapproval — this behaviour is not quite right
  • Amusement or gossip — look at all this drama
  • Mild scandal — people are doing things they probably shouldn't

When someone uses "goings-on," they are often hinting that the activities in question are a little shady, odd, or improper — even if they don't say so directly.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "There are some strange events happening at that office." — neutral, factual
  • "There are some strange goings-on at that office." — the same information, but now it sounds like you are half-suspicious, half-gossiping. There's a wink in the word.
It is always plural — without exception

You will never say "a going-on." The word simply does not exist in singular form. It is always goings-on, and it always takes a plural verb.

✅ These goings-on are very suspicious.
✅ The goings-on in that building worry me.
❌ This going-on is strange.
❌ A going-on occurred.
Register: who uses it, and when

Goings-on is informal and colloquial. It belongs to everyday speech and casual writing — not to formal reports, academic writing, or official documents.

It also has a slightly old-fashioned or traditional flavour. It's the kind of word a nosy neighbour, a gossipy aunt, or a disapproving elder might use. That said, it is still fully current and understood by all English speakers today. It's especially common in British English, though Americans use it too.

Goings-on is very frequently paired with adjectives that signal strangeness or suspicion:

  • strange goings-on
  • odd goings-on
  • mysterious goings-on
  • funny goings-on (funny here means suspicious, not humorous)
  • unsavoury goings-on
  • political goings-on
  • sexual goings-on

It is also common to say:

  • "I don't like these goings-on." (disapproval)
  • "She kept track of all the goings-on in the village." (gossiping/reporting)
  • "There were some interesting goings-on last night." (hinting at drama)

1. The neighbours noticed some suspicious goings-on at the old warehouse — men arriving late at night, lights flickering, boxes being unloaded.
→ Here it signals something shady and secretive.

2. She disapproved of the goings-on at her son's college parties.
→ Disapproval of behaviour she considers inappropriate.

3. The documentary gave viewers a fascinating look at the backstage goings-on of a royal palace.
→ More neutral here — just the behind-the-scenes activities — but still implies that these are things not usually seen or talked about.

4. "I don't know what goings-on you've been up to while I was away, but this house is a mess!"
→ Mild accusation, slightly humorous tone.

5. The journalist spent a year investigating the financial goings-on inside the corporation.
→ Implies irregular or questionable financial activities.

6. She sat by the window all day, watching the goings-on in the street below.
→ Just observing the activity and events of daily life — fairly neutral, more like people-watching.

• It does not mean the act of leaving or departing (even though "going" can mean that in other contexts). Here, it is completely unrelated to movement or travel.
  • It does not always mean something criminal — just something worth noting, and often something slightly irregular or unusual.

Imagine a gossipy person peering through their curtains, watching the neighbourhood, and later telling a friend: "Oh, you should have seen the goings-on next door last night!"

That image — of watchful curiosity, mild scandal, and the sense that something is happening that perhaps shouldn't be — is the heart of the word.

In one sentence: Goings-on means the (usually odd, suspicious, or noteworthy) events and activities happening in a place or situation — always used in the plural, always in an informal register, and almost always with a hint of curiosity or disapproval baked in.
6971: The noun gold digger has two meanings — one literal and one figurative. In everyday modern language, the figurative meaning is by far the more common and well-known one.
Meaning 1 — Literal: A Person Who Digs for Gold

In its most straightforward, physical sense, a gold digger is a person who literally digs in the earth searching for gold — a miner. This meaning was especially common in the 18th and 19th centuries during historical events like the California Gold Rush (1848–1855), when thousands of people moved to new regions hoping to find gold and become rich overnight.

Example:
"The gold diggers worked long hours in the river, hoping to find even a small nugget."

This meaning is rarely used today. When someone says "gold digger" in modern conversation, they almost always mean the second, figurative meaning below.
Meaning 2 — Figurative: A Person Who Pursues Wealth Through Relationships

This is the dominant, widely-used meaning today.

A gold digger is a person who deliberately enters into a romantic relationship — or maintains a close personal relationship — with someone else not out of genuine love, affection, or emotional connection, but primarily or entirely because that other person is wealthy.

In simple terms: they are attracted to your money, not to you.

The gold digger's core motivation is financial gain — getting access to money, gifts, expensive holidays, a luxurious lifestyle, property, or inheritance — through the relationship. The moment the money disappears, so does the gold digger.

Example:
"He realised she was a gold digger when she left him the moment he lost his job and his savings."
Key Characteristics of a Gold Digger

To truly understand the word, it helps to understand the specific behaviours and traits that define a gold digger:

1. Money is the primary motive.
A gold digger doesn't fall in love with a person — they fall in love with a person's bank account, lifestyle, or social status. Their affection is conditional on wealth.

2. The relationship is transactional.
They treat the relationship like a business deal. They offer company, romance, or loyalty in exchange for financial benefits — expensive gifts, paid bills, foreign trips, a nice home, or direct cash.

3. They specifically target wealthy individuals.
A gold digger is not simply someone who finds financial stability attractive (which is a normal, widespread preference). Instead, they deliberately seek out rich partners as a strategy, often showing little or no interest in people who are not wealthy.

4. Their feelings are largely fake or exaggerated.
They may appear very loving, very devoted, or very passionate — but this is often a performance designed to keep the wealthy partner emotionally hooked and financially generous.

5. They disappear when the money does.
One of the clearest signs of a gold digger is that their love evaporates the moment the financial benefit is gone. If the wealthy partner faces bankruptcy, loses their job, or stops spending money on the gold digger, the relationship ends — quickly.
Is It Always About a Romantic Relationship?

Mostly, yes — but not always. While the term is overwhelmingly used in a romantic or dating context, it can occasionally be used more loosely to describe anyone who befriends or associates with a person purely to extract money or material benefits from them, even outside of romance.

Example (non-romantic context):
"He was a real gold digger — he only stayed close to his wealthy uncle to be included in his will."

However, this looser usage is less common. The romantic context is the standard one.

Traditionally, the word has been used almost exclusively to describe women who pursue wealthy men. This reflects a long-standing cultural stereotype — and the word carries this historical bias in how it is typically used.

However, in modern usage, the word is not grammatically or logically restricted to women. A man can absolutely be called a gold digger if he pursues a wealthy woman (or a wealthy man) for financial gain. The behaviour, not the gender, is what defines the word. That said, when people use it without specifying gender, most listeners will still picture a woman, simply because of how deeply the stereotype is embedded in popular culture.

Absolutely. "Gold digger" is a strongly negative, derogatory term. Calling someone a gold digger is a serious insult. It implies that the person is:

  • Dishonest and deceptive
  • Manipulative
  • Materialistic
  • Selfish
  • Capable of faking love or affection for personal gain

It suggests a person has no real moral objection to exploiting another person's emotions and trust in order to live comfortably at their expense. Because of this, the word should be used carefully — it is a heavy accusation.
The Important Distinction: Gold Digger vs. Valuing Financial Stability

This is a crucial nuance that many people misunderstand.

Wanting a partner who is financially stable or responsible is completely normal and is NOT gold digging.

Most people, quite reasonably, prefer a partner who has a job, pays their bills, and can support themselves. That is a practical, healthy preference — not gold digging.

The difference lies in:

Normal PreferenceGold Digger
Attraction toThe whole person, including their character, personality, and financial stabilityThe money, almost exclusively
What happens if money disappearsStays in the relationshipLeaves the relationship
FeelingsGenuineLargely performed or manufactured
GoalA loving, stable relationshipAccess to wealth and material benefits

A gold digger would have no real interest in a partner if that partner were not rich. A person with a normal preference for stability would still value and love their partner even if circumstances changed financially.

• "His friends warned him that she was a gold digger, but he refused to believe it until she asked him to put her name on his property."
  • "People accused her of being a gold digger just because she married someone older and wealthier, which wasn't fair."
  • "The billionaire had a prenuptial agreement drawn up because he had been burned by a gold digger before."
  • "Don't be a gold digger — love people for who they are, not what they have."

A gold digger is a person who enters or maintains a romantic relationship primarily to gain access to another person's wealth, rather than out of genuine love — and who typically disappears the moment the money does.
6972:
A golden age is a period in history — or in any field — when things are at their absolute best. It is a time of great achievement, creativity, prosperity, and progress. Everything seems to be flourishing: ideas are bold, people are thriving, and the work being produced is exceptional.

Think of it like a bonfire. Most of the time, a fire burns steadily. But occasionally, it blazes so brightly and powerfully that everyone around it stops and stares. A golden age is that blazing moment — for a civilization, an art form, a sport, a science, or any area of human activity.

The term is ancient. It comes from Greek and Roman mythology, specifically from a poet named Hesiod, who lived around 700 BCE. In his work Works and Days, Hesiod described five stages of human history, each named after a metal:

  • The Golden Age — A time of peace, abundance, and harmony. Humans lived like gods: no war, no hunger, no suffering. The earth gave food freely, and people were just and good.
  • The Silver Age — A step down. People became foolish and stopped honoring the gods.
  • The Bronze Age — Violent and war-like.
  • The Heroic Age — The age of great heroes like Achilles and Odysseus.
  • The Iron Age — The worst of all. This, Hesiod said, was his era — full of toil, injustice, and misery.

The Roman poet Ovid later adopted and expanded this framework in his Metamorphoses, cementing the idea in Western culture.

So from the very beginning, the "golden age" sat at the top of the hierarchy. Gold, the most precious and enduring of metals, was the perfect symbol for the best period humanity could experience.

Gold is not just a metal. Throughout human history, across virtually every culture, gold has symbolized:

  • Purity — Gold doesn't rust, tarnish, or corrode. It stays perfect.
  • Rarity — It is difficult to find, which makes it precious.
  • Value — It has been used as the ultimate measure of worth for thousands of years.
  • Permanence — Gold lasts forever. Things made of gold endure.

When people call an era a "golden age," they are borrowing all of this symbolism. They are saying: this period was rare, precious, pure in its excellence, and its achievements will endure.
How the Term Is Used Today

Today, "golden age" has broken free from mythology and is used to describe any period of peak excellence in any domain — not just civilizations. It is one of the most versatile phrases in the English language.

Here are clear examples across different areas:

Civilizations and Empires:
The most classic use. The Golden Age of Ancient Greece (roughly 5th century BCE) was when Athens produced Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Parthenon, and the roots of democracy — all in a remarkably short span of time. The Islamic Golden Age (roughly 8th to 14th century CE) was when Muslim scholars in cities like Baghdad led the world in mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and philosophy, preserving and advancing knowledge while much of Europe was in the Dark Ages.

Art and Culture:
The Golden Age of Hollywood (roughly the 1930s–1960s) was when the American film industry produced iconic movies and stars at an astonishing rate — films that are still studied and celebrated today.

Literature:
The Golden Age of Science Fiction (roughly the 1930s–1950s) produced writers like Isaac Asimov, Arthur C. Clarke, and Robert Heinlein, who defined the genre for generations.

Sports:
People speak of the "golden age of tennis" or the "golden age of boxing" to describe periods when the sport was defined by a cluster of all-time-great competitors.

Technology:
Some argue we are currently living in a golden age of artificial intelligence or biotechnology — moments when rapid breakthroughs are redefining what is possible.

The pattern is always the same: a concentrated period where the quality, quantity, and impact of achievement is so extraordinary that it stands apart from everything before and after it.
The Most Important Feature: It Is Almost Always Recognized in Hindsight

This is a crucial and fascinating point about golden ages. People living through a golden age rarely know they're in one.

It is usually only after the period ends — sometimes decades or even centuries later — that people look back and say, "That was a golden age." This happens for a few reasons:

  1. Perspective requires distance. When you are in the middle of something, you cannot see its full shape. You only understand a mountain's height when you step away from it.
  2. Comparison is needed. A golden age only looks golden when you compare it to what came before and after. If the quality drops after a certain period, the period before the drop starts to shine in memory.
  3. Nostalgia plays a role. Human memory tends to romanticize the past. We remember the highlights of a previous era more than its flaws, which makes it seem even more golden over time.

There are exceptions — some people do recognize greatness in real time — but the retrospective quality is what makes golden ages feel so wistful and poetic.

No single ingredient creates a golden age, but historians and thinkers have identified common conditions that tend to produce them:

  • Stability and peace — When people are not fighting for survival, they have energy to create, think, and innovate.
  • Wealth and patronage — Resources allow artists, scientists, and thinkers to pursue their work. The Italian Renaissance's golden age, for example, was fueled by wealthy patrons like the Medici family who funded artists like Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo.
  • The free flow of ideas — Golden ages often occur when cultures are open, when trade routes bring in diverse influences, or when censorship is low.
  • A critical mass of talent — Sometimes, by circumstance, many brilliant individuals happen to be alive and working at the same time, inspiring and competing with each other.
  • A problem that needs solving — Necessity can drive extraordinary innovation. Wartime, for example, accelerated the golden age of aviation and computing.

They always do. Every golden age eventually fades, and it ends for various reasons:

  • Invasion or war — External forces destroy the conditions that allowed flourishing. The Islamic Golden Age, for instance, was devastated by the Mongol invasion of 1258, which destroyed Baghdad.
  • Economic decline — When the money runs out, the patronage and infrastructure that supported the golden age collapse.
  • Internal decay — Institutions become corrupt, social cohesion breaks down, or the culture becomes complacent.
  • The natural exhaustion of a movement — In art and culture, styles and ideas eventually run their course. A genre that was fresh and exciting becomes formulaic.
  • Changing context — Sometimes the world simply moves on, and the conditions that made a golden age possible no longer exist.

The end of a golden age does not mean everything gets permanently worse — it simply means that particular peak has passed, and a new trajectory begins.
The Philosophical Dimension: Is the "Golden Age" Real or a Myth?

This is where things get intellectually interesting. Some scholars argue that "golden ages" are partly a myth of nostalgia — that people idealize the past because the present always feels harder and more complicated to live through. By this view, every generation thinks the previous one was a golden age, while ignoring its real problems.

For example, those who romanticize the Golden Age of Hollywood often overlook that it was an era of racial segregation, rigid censorship, and the suppression of women. Ancient Athens, for all its philosophy and democracy, was a slave-owning society that excluded women from public life entirely.

The truth is somewhere in the middle:

  • Yes, certain periods genuinely produced extraordinary concentrations of achievement.
  • But no golden age was perfect — every one had deep flaws and injustices running alongside its greatness.
  • And yes, nostalgia causes us to polish the image of the past, making golden ages seem shinier than they truly were.

Understanding this doesn't diminish the concept — it makes it richer. A golden age is real and a construction of memory, both at the same time.
Quick Summary — Everything in One Paragraph

A golden age is any period — in a civilization, an art form, a science, a sport, or any domain — during which achievement, creativity, and excellence reach an extraordinary peak. The term comes from ancient Greek and Roman mythology, where the "Golden Age" was the first and best era of human existence, characterized by peace and abundance. Gold was chosen as the symbol because of its purity, rarity, and permanence. Golden ages are usually recognized in hindsight, after the period has ended, and they typically arise from a combination of stability, wealth, talent, and the free flow of ideas. They always end, often due to war, economic decline, or the simple exhaustion of a movement. And while they are real, they are also partly shaped by nostalgia — our tendency to remember the best of the past and forget the rest.

That is everything there is to know about the term "golden age" — from its mythological roots to its philosophical complexity, applied across history and human experience.
6973:
A golden handshake is a large, generous financial payment given to a senior executive or employee when they leave a company — whether they are fired, forced to retire, or choose to leave as part of a deal.

Think of it as the company's way of saying: "Here is a big goodbye gift for your years of service and loyalty."
Breaking Down the Name

The word "golden" means valuable, generous, and financially rich. In the business world, anything "golden" refers to a high-value financial deal or benefit given to top-level people.

The word "handshake" traditionally symbolizes an agreement or a farewell between two parties. When you shake hands with someone leaving, it marks the end of a relationship.

Put them together — golden handshake — and you get a rich, generous farewell deal between a company and a departing employee.
Who Gets a Golden Handshake?

Golden handshakes are not for ordinary employees. They are typically reserved for:

  • CEOs (Chief Executive Officers)
  • CFOs (Chief Financial Officers)
  • Board members and directors
  • Senior executives and top-level managers

Basically, the higher up you are in a company, the more likely you are to receive one. A regular office worker or factory employee would not typically receive a golden handshake. They might receive a standard severance package, which is far more modest and routine.
What Does a Golden Handshake Actually Include?

A golden handshake is rarely just a single cheque. It is usually a package of financial benefits bundled together. It can include any combination of the following:

Lump-sum cash payment. This is the most straightforward part — a direct, one-time payment of money. This amount can be in the hundreds of thousands, or even millions of dollars (or any other currency), depending on the executive's seniority and the terms of their contract.

Stock or shares in the company. The executive may be given company stocks as part of the deal, which they can hold or sell. Since senior executives often already own company shares, this can be enormously valuable.

Pension benefits. The package often includes a boosted pension — meaning the executive receives more retirement money than they would have if they had simply resigned normally.

Continued health insurance or medical benefits. Even after leaving the company, the departing executive may continue to receive health coverage for a period of time.

Extended use of company perks. Things like a company car, private jet access, housing allowance, or club memberships might continue for a defined period post-departure.

Consulting fees. Sometimes companies agree to pay the departing executive as a "consultant" for a period after they leave, even if the person does little to no actual consulting work. This is often a way to spread out the payout and make it look more acceptable.

Not every golden handshake includes all of these — the exact composition depends on what was agreed upon in the executive's original employment contract.
The Key Point: It Is Often Pre-Agreed

This is crucial to understand. In most cases, a golden handshake is not a surprise bonus invented on the day someone leaves. It is typically written into the executive's contract from the very beginning, before they even start the job.

When a company hires a powerful CEO, for example, the CEO's lawyer and the company's lawyer negotiate an entire employment agreement. Buried within that agreement is often a severance clause — a section that spells out exactly what happens financially if the executive leaves or is removed. This pre-agreed payout is the golden handshake.

This matters because it means the company legally agreed to pay this amount upfront, long before the departure ever happened. It is a binding obligation, not a voluntary gift.
Why Do Companies Offer Golden Handshakes?

From the company's point of view, offering a golden handshake makes sense for several reasons.

To attract top talent. The most skilled and sought-after executives have enormous choices. Competing companies all want them. By promising a generous exit package in the event things don't work out, a company makes itself more attractive to hire. It reassures the executive: "Even if this goes wrong, you will be taken care of."

To remove someone cleanly and quickly. When a company needs to remove a CEO — perhaps because the company is underperforming, or because there is a strategic shift — it wants the process to be fast and quiet. A large financial settlement encourages the departing person to leave without creating legal battles, negative publicity, or bitter public disputes. Money smooths the exit.

To enforce silence. Golden handshake agreements almost always come with a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), which legally prevents the departing executive from speaking negatively about the company, sharing internal secrets, or criticising the board in public. The golden handshake essentially buys the executive's silence and cooperation.

To prevent the person from joining a rival. The agreement may include a non-compete clause, which prevents the departing executive from working for a competing company for a set period of time — often one to two years. The golden handshake financially compensates them for this period during which they cannot work in their industry.

To honour a legal and moral obligation. If the company is restructuring, merging, or downsizing and must lay off its executive leadership — even when those executives did nothing wrong — the golden handshake is simply the fair and agreed-upon compensation for ending the contract early.
Two Main Scenarios Where It Happens

Golden handshakes occur in two broad situations:

1. Involuntary departure (the company pushes the person out)

This is the most common scenario. The board of directors decides they want a new CEO, or the company merges with another organisation and there is no longer a need for the current executive. The person is not being fired for doing something wrong — they are simply being let go due to business circumstances. The golden handshake rewards them for their service and compensates them for the sudden loss of their job.

2. Voluntary early retirement

Sometimes a company wants to reduce its workforce during tough economic times. Instead of mass redundancies at the lower levels, they encourage senior (and often highly-paid) employees to retire early by sweetening the deal. They essentially say: "If you agree to retire now rather than in five years, we will give you a very generous payout." This benefits the company by reducing payroll costs, and benefits the employee by securing their financial future ahead of schedule.
The Controversy Around Golden Handshakes

Golden handshakes are deeply controversial, and this is where it gets interesting.

The core criticism is that executives sometimes receive enormous golden handshakes even when they have performed poorly — or even when their decisions actively harmed the company and its shareholders. Critics argue this rewards failure, which is fundamentally unfair. It sends the message: "You can run this company into the ground, and we'll still pay you millions on your way out."

Imagine a CEO who leads a company for three years, during which the company's share price falls dramatically, thousands of employees are laid off, and profits collapse. That CEO is then removed by the board — and walks away with a $20 million golden handshake. Shareholders, employees, and the general public often find this deeply unjust.

The other major criticism is the sheer scale of these packages. While an ordinary worker might receive a few weeks of redundancy pay when they lose their job, a senior executive receives what is often a life-changing sum. This disparity fuels anger about inequality within corporations.

However, defenders of golden handshakes make a valid counter-argument. They say that:

  • The amounts were agreed upon in a legal contract, and contracts must be honoured.
  • The packages are necessary to attract world-class talent.
  • Without such protection, the best executives would never take the risk of leaving a secure position to lead a large company.
  • Not all golden handshakes are for poor performers — many are simply the cost of a necessary organisational change.
A Golden Handshake vs. Standard Redundancy Pay — What's the Difference?

When any regular employee is made redundant (let go due to the role being eliminated rather than poor performance), they usually receive standard redundancy pay, which is a modest, legally mandated amount based on their years of service and salary. It follows a fixed formula set by law.

A golden handshake, on the other hand, is negotiated individually, is almost always much larger than standard redundancy pay, and is given to senior figures as part of a bespoke contractual agreement. It is not a legal requirement — it is a privately negotiated deal. The two are entirely different in scale and nature.
The Golden Family: Related Terms You Should Know

The business world has several "golden" terms, and confusing them is very common. Here is a clear distinction:

Golden Handshake — A large payout when a senior executive leaves the company (departure benefit).

Golden Parachute — Very similar to a golden handshake, but the term is specifically used when an executive loses their job due to a company takeover or acquisition. It is the financial cushion that softens the fall when one company buys another and the old leadership is replaced. The two terms are often used interchangeably, but technically a golden parachute is a subset of the golden handshake concept, specifically tied to mergers and acquisitions.

Golden Handcuffs — This is the opposite concept. Instead of a leaving payment, golden handcuffs are financial incentives designed to keep an employee at the company. These might include bonuses that only pay out after five years of service, stock options that vest gradually, or special benefits that disappear if the employee resigns. They "handcuff" the person to the company by making it financially painful to leave.

Golden Hello — This is a large signing bonus paid when an executive joins a company, to entice them away from their current employer. It is the welcome gift, whereas the golden handshake is the farewell gift.

So the full lifecycle looks like this: a company pays a golden hello to bring someone in, golden handcuffs to keep them there, and a golden handshake to let them go.
A Simple Real-World Example to Cement Your Understanding

Imagine a large technology company — let's call it TechCorp — that hires a new CEO named Sarah. When Sarah is hired, her contract states:

"If Sarah is removed from her role or if the company is sold within the first five years, she will receive a lump-sum payment of $15 million, plus two years of health insurance, plus immediate vesting of all her company shares."

Three years later, TechCorp is acquired by a larger company. Sarah's role is eliminated. She walks away with the $15 million, her health insurance, and her shares — all of which were already promised to her in her contract. That is her golden handshake.

Was it fair? That depends on who you ask. But it was legal, contractual, and agreed upon by both parties from the very beginning.
The Core Takeaway

A golden handshake is a pre-negotiated, large financial exit package given to high-ranking executives when they depart a company — voluntarily or otherwise. It exists because top executives command enormous bargaining power, companies need to attract and smoothly remove leadership, and business contracts are binding agreements that must be honoured.

It rewards the executive for their service, compensates them for losing their position, purchases their silence and cooperation, and prevents messy, public legal battles. Whether it is just or unjust is one of the great ongoing debates in corporate governance — but there is no doubt that golden handshakes remain a standard feature of executive-level employment across the world.
6974:
Imagine you are the CEO of a big company. One day, a larger company decides to buy your company. When that happens, the new owners often bring in their own team — which means you might lose your job through no fault of your own.

A golden parachute is a promise made to you before any of this happens, written into your employment contract, that says: "If you ever lose your job because someone buys or takes over this company, we will give you a very large financial package on your way out."

Just like a parachute saves a pilot who has to jump out of a plane, a golden parachute financially "saves" an executive who is forced out of their company. And just like the word "golden" suggests — it is extremely generous.

Golden parachutes are not for regular employees. They are reserved for the highest-ranking executives in a company, typically:

  • The CEO (Chief Executive Officer — the top boss)
  • The CFO (Chief Financial Officer — the head of finances)
  • The COO (Chief Operating Officer — who runs day-to-day operations)
  • Other members of the C-suite (senior leadership team)

These are the people who have the most to lose when a company changes hands, because new owners almost always want to install their own leadership. A golden parachute is essentially a form of job-loss insurance, but one that pays out at a scale that most ordinary people can barely imagine.
What Is Actually Inside a Golden Parachute?

A golden parachute is not just one thing — it is a package of financial benefits. The exact contents vary from company to company and are negotiated when the executive is first hired or when their contract is renewed. Common components include:

Cash severance pay. This is a lump sum of money paid to the executive upon departure. It is often calculated as a multiple of the executive's annual salary — commonly two to three times their yearly pay. For a CEO earning $5 million a year, that could mean a $10–15 million cash payment just for leaving.

Accelerated vesting of stock options and restricted stock. Many executives are compensated partly in company stock, which they are only allowed to "collect" (or vest) over a period of years. Under a golden parachute, all that stock vests immediately upon departure, rather than making the executive wait. This can be worth tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars.

Continuation of benefits. This includes maintaining health insurance, life insurance, and other perks for an extended period after the executive leaves — sometimes for years.

Pension enhancements. The executive may receive a larger pension or retirement benefit than they would have earned under normal circumstances.

Bonuses. Sometimes a golden parachute includes payment of annual bonuses that the executive would have received if they had stayed.

All of these together can add up to a staggering amount. It is not rare for a golden parachute to be worth $20 million, $50 million, or even more.
When Is a Golden Parachute Triggered?

Golden parachutes do not pay out just because an executive feels like quitting. They are triggered by very specific events, almost always related to a change of control of the company. This typically means:

  • A merger — when two companies combine into one
  • An acquisition — when one company buys another
  • A hostile takeover — when a company is bought against the wishes of its current management

Even within these events, the golden parachute is usually only triggered if the executive is also fired or forced to resign after the takeover. If the executive willingly stays on and works happily for the new owners, the parachute generally does not open.

Many contracts contain a clause called "double trigger" — meaning two things must both happen for the payout to kick in: (1) the company must be taken over, AND (2) the executive must lose their job or be forced into a significantly worse role. This is contrasted with a "single trigger" clause, where just the takeover alone is enough to trigger the payout, even if the executive keeps their job.
Why Do Companies Offer Golden Parachutes?

This is where it gets really interesting — because companies do not offer golden parachutes out of pure kindness. There are several very practical, strategic reasons.

Attracting top talent. Running a major corporation is an incredibly demanding job. The very best executives have many options. A golden parachute is part of a competitive compensation package that companies use to lure the most capable leaders.

Keeping executives focused. Without a golden parachute, a CEO whose company is being taken over might spend all their energy trying to protect their own job — making decisions that benefit themselves rather than the shareholders. With a golden parachute in place, the executive knows they will be financially fine no matter what, so they can focus on getting the best possible deal for the company's owners.

Making hostile takeovers more expensive. A golden parachute raises the cost of buying a company, because the acquiring company must pay out these large packages. This acts as a mild deterrent to unwanted takeover attempts, giving the current management and board more time to evaluate whether a deal is genuinely good for the company.

Let's say Sarah is the CEO of a mid-sized technology company. When she was hired, she negotiated a golden parachute into her contract. It states that if the company is acquired and she loses her job as a result, she will receive:

  • 3× her annual $4 million salary = $12 million in cash
  • Immediate vesting of all her stock options, currently worth $30 million
  • Health insurance for 3 years, valued at roughly $150,000

Total golden parachute: approximately $42 million.

A large tech giant acquires Sarah's company. The new owners install their own CEO. Sarah walks out the door with $42 million. That is her golden parachute.
The Controversy — Why Critics Dislike Golden Parachutes

Golden parachutes are one of the most debated topics in corporate governance, and the criticism is fierce and largely justified. Here is why many people — including economists, shareholders, and the general public — take issue with them:

They can reward failure. Imagine a CEO who made terrible decisions that drove the company's value down so far that it became an easy acquisition target. Under a golden parachute, that CEO might still walk away with $30–50 million. Critics argue this is rewarding the very person who destroyed value.

They harm shareholders. The money paid out in golden parachutes comes, directly or indirectly, from the company — which means it reduces the value that flows to the actual owners of the company (the shareholders). Shareholders sometimes feel they are paying executives to leave a mess behind.

The amounts seem disproportionate. When a factory worker is laid off, they might receive a few weeks of severance pay. When a CEO is let go, they might receive $50 million. The sheer scale of the disparity strikes many as deeply unfair and disconnected from any reasonable notion of merit.

They may discourage executives from fighting bad deals. Ironically, a golden parachute can sometimes make an executive too comfortable with a takeover — even a bad one — because they know they will be richly compensated regardless of what happens to the company or its employees afterward.
How Governments and Regulators Have Responded

Because of these controversies, lawmakers have put some guardrails in place — though critics argue they do not go nearly far enough.

Tax penalties in the U.S. Under the U.S. Internal Revenue Code (specifically Sections 280G and 4999), if a golden parachute payout exceeds three times the executive's average annual compensation from the previous five years, the excess amount is subject to a 20% excise tax — on top of regular income tax. The company also loses the ability to deduct that excess as a business expense. This makes very large parachutes more costly, but it has not eliminated them.

Shareholder approval ("Say on Pay"). In the United States, under the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010, shareholders of public companies have the right to vote on golden parachute arrangements in connection with mergers and acquisitions. However, this vote is typically non-binding — meaning companies can ignore it.

Disclosure requirements. Public companies are required to fully disclose the details of golden parachute agreements to the public through filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). This transparency allows shareholders and the press to scrutinize these deals.

You will often hear similar-sounding terms in the business world. Here is how they differ:

Silver parachute. Similar concept, but for a broader group of employees — not just the top executives but also mid-level managers. The payouts are smaller than a golden parachute.

Tin parachute. Extends some departure benefits to regular, non-management employees in the event of a takeover. The amounts are far more modest.

Golden handcuffs. This is essentially the opposite concept in spirit. Golden handcuffs are financial incentives (like stock that vests over many years) designed to keep an executive at a company rather than to pay them on their way out.

Golden handshake. This term is sometimes used interchangeably with golden parachute, but more precisely it refers to a generous retirement package or exit deal that may or may not be tied to a takeover — sometimes it simply refers to a negotiated buyout of an employment contract.

A golden parachute is a pre-negotiated, extremely generous financial safety net built into the employment contract of top corporate executives. It activates when the executive loses their job due to a company merger, acquisition, or hostile takeover. It typically consists of large cash payments, accelerated stock vesting, and continued benefits. Companies offer them to attract talent, keep executives focused, and deter hostile takeovers. But they are deeply controversial because they can richly reward failure, come at shareholders' expense, and highlight the stark inequality between how regular workers and top executives are treated when a company changes hands. Governments have introduced some tax and disclosure measures to temper them, but golden parachutes remain a permanent — and polarizing — fixture of corporate life.
6975:
A golem is an artificial creature — most often shaped like a human — that has been brought to life through magical or mystical means, rather than through natural birth. It is not born; it is made and then activated. It moves, it acts, it follows orders — but it has no soul, no true inner life, and no will of its own.

Think of it as a living puppet made of clay: it walks and works, but there is nobody truly home inside.

The golem comes from Jewish folklore and mystical tradition. The most famous story is the Golem of Prague. According to the legend, a rabbi in 16th-century Prague shaped a figure out of river clay — tall, powerful, humanoid — and brought it to life by writing a sacred Hebrew word on its forehead (or placing a piece of parchment inscribed with a holy name into its mouth). The golem was created for one purpose: to protect the Jewish community from violent attacks.

To deactivate it, the rabbi simply erased one letter from its forehead, and the creature collapsed, lifeless once again.

This story captures everything essential about what a golem is:

  • Artificially made (not born)
  • Brought to life by a person with special knowledge or power
  • Powerful but obedient — a servant, not a thinking being
  • Can be "turned off" by its creator
  • Created for a specific purpose
What makes a golem different from other creatures

It helps to compare the golem to things we're more familiar with:

A golem is not a ghost or spirit. A ghost is a soul that persists after death. A golem never had a soul in the first place.

A golem is not a monster. Monsters (in most stories) act on their own instincts or desires. A golem has no desires. It doesn't want anything. It just does what it's told.

A golem is not a human. Even though it looks human and moves like one, it cannot speak (in most versions of the lore), cannot think for itself, and has no emotions. It is the shape of a person without the inner life of one.

The closest modern comparison would be a robot — but one made of clay and magic rather than metal and circuits. In fact, the golem is considered one of the earliest imaginative ancestors of the robot and the concept of artificial intelligence.
The deeper idea the word carries

The golem isn't just a creature — it represents a powerful and unsettling idea: what happens when a person tries to create life?

In almost every golem story, there is an undercurrent of warning. The golem serves faithfully at first, but it can become uncontrollable. If the creator loses control, the golem may go on a rampage — not out of malice, but because it has no judgment. It only knows how to act; it doesn't know when to stop. It is brute force without wisdom.

This is why the golem is often seen as a symbol of:

  • The dangers of playing God — creating something you may not be able to control
  • Power without conscience — strength that exists without moral understanding
  • The gap between mechanical action and true intelligence — doing something is not the same as understanding what you're doing
How the word is used more broadly

Over centuries, the meaning of "golem" has expanded beyond its folkloric origin. Today, you might encounter it used in several ways:

1. In fantasy, mythology, and gaming:
Golems appear everywhere in fantasy fiction, role-playing games (like Dungeons & Dragons), and video games. In these contexts, a golem is almost any kind of magically animated construct — made of stone, iron, wood, ice, flesh, or other materials. The core idea remains the same: an artificial being made to serve, with no independent mind.

2. As a metaphor for a person:
Calling someone a "golem" (especially in informal or literary use) implies they are slow-witted, clumsy, lumbering, or mechanical in their behavior — someone who follows instructions without thinking, or who acts like a mindless automaton. It's not a flattering comparison.

3. As a metaphor for any system or creation:
More broadly, "golem" can refer to any creation — institution, system, or entity — that was built to serve a purpose but has grown beyond the control of its creators, or that operates without true understanding or moral judgment.
The essential qualities of a golem, summarized

No matter the context, when something is called a golem, it typically means:

  • It was created, not born
  • It was animated by external magical or supernatural force
  • It is humanoid or human-like in form
  • It lacks a soul, consciousness, or free will
  • It obeys its maker (until it doesn't)
  • It is powerful but mindless
  • It can become dangerous when control is lost

The golem had a profound influence on later storytelling. Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) — in which a scientist creates a being from dead matter and brings it to life — is deeply indebted to golem mythology. So are nearly all stories about robots, androids, and artificial intelligence that grapple with the question: if we build something that acts like it's alive, is it really alive? And what do we owe it — or fear from it?

The golem, in this sense, is not just a word. It is an ancient lens through which human beings have long examined their own desire to create, control, and the uncomfortable consequences that follow.
6976: The word gondola refers to several distinct things in English, but there's a quiet thread connecting most of them: a container or compartment that is carried, suspended, or floated. Once you see that thread, the word becomes much easier to remember across all its uses.
1. The Venetian Boat (The Most Famous Meaning)

When most people hear "gondola," they picture this: a long, narrow, flat-bottomed boat that glides through the canals of Venice, Italy. It has a distinctive curved shape — the front and back both rise upward in a graceful arc, and the boat is slightly asymmetrical (one side is a little wider than the other), which helps it move in a straight line when pushed from just one side.A gondola is steered and propelled by a single person called a gondolier, who stands at the rear (back) of the boat and pushes through the water using a long oar. The oar rests in a special wooden bracket on the side of the boat — the gondolier doesn't paddle alternately from side to side like a canoe; instead, they use a sweeping, twisting motion from one fixed position.

Gondolas are traditionally painted black (this became a rule centuries ago to prevent wealthy families from competing with each other through flashy decorations). They typically have a decorative metal ornament at the front called a ferro — a comb-like piece of metal whose six prongs are said by some to represent the six districts of Venice.

Today, gondolas in Venice are primarily used for tourist rides, though they were once the main everyday transport for Venetians, before motorboats took over.
2. The Cable Car Cabin (Very Common in Modern Use)

This is probably the second most common meaning you'll encounter. A gondola is the enclosed, cabin-like compartment that hangs from a cable and carries passengers up and down mountains or across valleys. You see these at ski resorts, mountain tourist attractions, and even some cities.The cabin itself is what's called the gondola — not the whole cable system, just the box or pod that hangs from the cable and travels along it. These gondolas are usually fully enclosed (with windows and a door), can carry several passengers at once, and are attached to the moving cable overhead. They travel continuously or in a loop, picking up and dropping off passengers at stations.

You might also hear these called cable cars, aerial trams, or ropeways, but when someone specifically says "gondola" in this context, they mean the hanging passenger cabin — the compartment itself.

When a hot air balloon floats through the sky, the people inside are not standing in the balloon itself — they're standing in a basket or compartment that hangs below the balloon. That basket is called a gondola.

The same word is used for the passenger compartment beneath a blimp or airship (like the Goodyear Blimp) — the enclosed cabin that hangs underneath the gas-filled envelope where pilots and passengers sit.

In both cases, the gondola is the habitable part — where humans are — suspended beneath the lifting part (the balloon or the gas bag).

In the world of railways and freight transport, a gondola (also called a gondola car or gondola railcar) is a type of freight wagon — a long, flat-bottomed, open-top railcar with low walls on the sides and ends.

Think of it like a big rectangular tub on wheels. Because the top is completely open, it's used to carry loose bulk materials that don't need protection from the weather: things like coal, gravel, scrap metal, sand, or ore. You load them in from the top with a crane or conveyor, and you can unload them by tipping the car or using machinery.

This type of railcar is extremely common in freight rail networks, particularly in North America.

Walk into almost any supermarket or large retail store, and look at the freestanding shelf units that run down the middle of the aisles — the ones you can access from both sides. In the retail and merchandising industry, those double-sided shelving structures are called gondolas (or gondola shelving).A gondola in a store consists of a central upright frame with adjustable shelves extending outward on both sides. Store managers talk about things like "end-cap gondolas" (the shelves at the end of an aisle, which are especially valuable display spots) and use the word routinely when planning store layouts. This meaning of the word is mostly used by people in the retail and grocery industries, not everyday shoppers — but you will encounter it if you ever work in retail or read about store design.

Here's a simple way to hold all of this in your head:

  • Venice → the iconic long black boat gliding through canals
  • Mountains / ski resorts → the enclosed cabin hanging from a cable overhead
  • Hot air balloons / blimps → the basket or cabin hanging below the balloon
  • Railways → the open-top freight wagon used to carry bulk cargo
  • Supermarkets → the double-sided freestanding shelf units in store aisles

The first three share a genuine conceptual link: in each, the gondola is a compartment that is either floating on water or suspended in the air, carrying people or goods. The freight railcar and the retail shelving share the shape — a flat-bottomed, open, tub-like structure — with the Venetian boat. That's why the same word stretched to cover all of these over time.

In everyday life, you're most likely to encounter "gondola" meaning the Venetian boat, the cable car cabin, or (if you're in the retail industry) the store shelving.
6977:
"Gone are the days" means that a certain time, era, or situation that once existed no longer exists. It is a way of saying that something which used to be true, common, or normal in the past has now ended — it belongs to history, not to the present.

Think of it like pointing to the past and saying: "That time is over. It doesn't happen anymore."
Breaking Down the Words

The expression is beautifully simple when you look at it word by word.

"Gone" means disappeared, finished, or no longer here. When something is gone, it has left and is not coming back — or at least, it is not here now.

"The days" refers to a period of time — not just one 24-hour day, but an entire era or phase in life when things were a certain way.

Put them together: "Gone are the days" = "Those times have disappeared."
Why Is the Word Order Reversed?

If you look at this phrase carefully, you will notice something unusual. In normal English, we say:

"The days are gone." — Subject (The days) → Verb (are gone)

But in this expression, the order is flipped:

"Gone are the days." — Verb first (Gone) → Subject after (the days)

This reversal is called inversion, and it is done deliberately. In English, when you bring a word to the very front of a sentence, it gets extra emphasis and dramatic weight. By placing "gone" at the very beginning, the speaker puts full emotional focus on the fact that something has ended. It makes the sentence feel more powerful, poetic, and expressive than simply saying "the days are gone."

This is why you will often see this expression in speeches, literature, song lyrics, and emotional conversations — places where people want their words to carry more feeling.
What Comes After the Expression

The expression is almost never used alone. It is typically followed by one of two things:

1. "When" + a description of what used to happen

This is the most common pattern. You describe the past situation after the word "when."

  • "Gone are the days when people had to visit a library to find information."
  • "Gone are the days when children played outside from morning until dark."
  • "Gone are the days when a letter took two weeks to arrive."

2. "Of" + a noun

Here, instead of a full sentence, you use a noun (a thing or idea) to describe what has ended.

  • "Gone are the days of affordable housing."
  • "Gone are the days of simple, quiet mornings."
  • "Gone are the days of trust between neighbors."

Both patterns work perfectly. Choose "when" when you want to describe an action or situation. Choose "of" when you want to refer to a concept, a thing, or a general era.
The Tone and Emotion Behind It

One of the most interesting things about this expression is that it can carry very different emotions depending on the speaker and the situation. The words themselves are neutral, but the context gives them their feeling.

Nostalgia and Wistfulness — This is the most common tone. The speaker misses the old days and feels a gentle sadness that they are over.

"Gone are the days when the whole family would gather around one radio to listen together." — Here, the speaker clearly misses that warmth and togetherness.

Relief and Gladness — Sometimes the speaker is happy that those days are gone, because the past was difficult, unjust, or inconvenient.

"Gone are the days when women were not allowed to vote." — Here, the tone is one of progress and relief.

"Gone are the days when I had to wake up at 5 a.m. for my old job." — Here, the speaker is simply glad things have changed.

Neutral Observation — Sometimes the speaker is not nostalgic or relieved, just simply noting that times have changed.

"Gone are the days when people memorized phone numbers. Now everything is stored in a phone."

So when you hear or read this expression, pay attention to the context. The same structure can express very different feelings.
Real-Life Examples in Full Sentences

Here are some natural, everyday examples that show you how the expression is actually used:

"Gone are the days when you had to go to a travel agent to book a flight. Now you can do it in minutes from your phone."

"Gone are the days of hand-written recipes passed from mother to daughter. Everything is now on the internet."

"He looked at the old neighborhood and sighed. Gone are the days when every door on this street was left unlocked."

"Gone are the days when you could buy a house in the city for a reasonable price."

"Gone are the days of waiting in long queues at the bank — online banking has changed everything."

Notice how each sentence paints a clear contrast between then and now. The expression always implies a "before and after" — a time when something was one way, and a present where it is no longer that way.
What the Expression Is NOT Saying

It is important to understand what this phrase does not mean, so you don't misuse it.

It does not mean that something happened for a very short time. It refers to a whole era or period — a stretch of time during which something was consistently true or common.

It does not always mean forever. Sometimes people use it casually to describe a change in habit or lifestyle, not necessarily a permanent shift in the world.

It is not used for things happening right now or in the future. It is always looking backward.
How Is It Different From Simply Saying "That Doesn't Happen Anymore"?

You could always say, "People don't write letters by hand anymore." That is perfectly clear and correct.

But "Gone are the days when people wrote letters by hand" does something richer. It acknowledges that there was a whole era — a distinct chapter in time — when that was the norm. It gives that past era a sense of weight and significance. It says: "There was a real time when this was a different world, and that world has closed."

This is why the expression feels more emotional and reflective than a plain factual statement. It does not just report a change — it pauses to acknowledge it.
Formal or Informal? Where Will You Hear It?

This expression sits comfortably in both formal and informal settings, though it leans slightly toward the literary or reflective side of language.

You will encounter it in books, novels, and essays. You will hear it in speeches — politicians and leaders often use it to talk about how times have changed. You will find it in journalism, especially in opinion pieces about society and culture. You will also hear it in everyday conversation when someone is feeling nostalgic or reflective.

It is not slang, and it is not overly formal. Think of it as sitting in the comfortable middle ground — expressive and slightly poetic, but not stuffy or academic.
A Useful Variation to Know

You will sometimes hear people say "those were the days" — a related but different expression. While "gone are the days" focuses on the fact that a time has ended, "those were the days" is more purely nostalgic, fondly looking back at good times from the past. They are close cousins but not identical.
A Simple Way to Remember It Forever

Here is a mental image to lock this expression in your memory:

Imagine an old photograph. In it, you can see a moment from the past — people dressed differently, living differently, doing things in a way no one does anymore. You hold that photograph and say: "Gone are the days when life looked like this."

The photograph is the past. The fading of it is the "gone." And the expression is your way of holding both feelings at once — the recognition that time has moved on, and the acknowledgment that it once was a certain way.

In one sentence: "Gone are the days" is an expression that means a particular time or situation from the past no longer exists today — used to reflect on how much things have changed, with a tone that can be nostalgic, relieved, or simply observational.
6978: "Goo-goo" as an adjective describes two closely related things: a look of silly, dreamy infatuation, and anything resembling the soft, meaningless sounds a baby makes. Both meanings share the same feeling — something unguarded, sweet, and a little silly.
Meaning 1: Lovesick and Adoring (The Main Use)

This is by far the most common adjectival use of the word. When you describe someone's eyes or expression as "goo-goo," you mean they are looking at someone with a helplessly adoring, dreamy, starry-eyed gaze — the kind of look that makes it completely obvious that the person is head over heels in love or deeply infatuated.

Think of a teenager who has just fallen for someone and can't stop staring at them with wide, soft, almost glazed eyes. Their expression is melting, tender, and a bit silly — not sharp or composed. That is a goo-goo look.

The most classic phrase: "making goo-goo eyes" — this means gazing at someone with obvious romantic adoration or infatuation, often in a way that others around you can clearly notice (and perhaps find a little embarrassing or amusing).

Examples:

  • "He sat across from her the whole dinner, making goo-goo eyes and barely touching his food."
  • "Stop giving me those goo-goo looks — everyone at the table can see you."
  • "She had a goo-goo expression on her face every time his name came up."

The feeling it carries: It's affectionate but slightly teasing. When you call someone's look "goo-goo," you're acknowledging that their affection is genuine but also that it looks a bit silly or mushy to an outside observer. It's not an insult — it's more of a light, warm, humorous observation. It suggests the person is so smitten that they've lost a little of their composure.

The second meaning connects to the literal sounds babies make — "goo-goo, ga-ga." When used as an adjective in this sense, "goo-goo" describes something that is childlike, babbling, or infantile in nature — speech, behavior, or sounds that resemble what you'd hear from or direct toward a very young baby.

Examples:

  • "She spoke to her puppy in a goo-goo voice, saying things like 'Who's a good boy?'"
  • "The adults started talking in goo-goo tones the moment they saw the newborn."
  • "His goo-goo noises made the baby laugh."

This meaning is often used when adults "baby-talk" — either to actual babies, to pets, or (sometimes playfully) to people they are very fond of. The word captures the soft, cooing, high-pitched, nonsensical quality of that kind of speech.

Both meanings share a common thread: a loss of the normal, composed, "adult" guard. Whether you're gazing adoringly at your crush or cooing at a baby, you're in a state of soft, unguarded, unselfconscious affection. "Goo-goo" captures that sweet, slightly ridiculous loosening of composure that comes with strong tender feeling.

"Goo-goo" is a casual, informal, conversational word. You would use it in everyday speech, friendly writing, or light-hearted contexts. It is not a word you'd find in formal writing or serious situations. It almost always carries a playful or gently teasing tone — even when used affectionately. Nobody says "goo-goo" with a straight, serious face.

It can be used affectionately ("Aww, look at him making goo-goo eyes at her — so cute") or with mild mockery ("Don't go all goo-goo just because he smiled at you"), but in both cases the feeling is light and warm rather than harsh.

UseWhat It MeansTypical Phrase
About a look/expressionDreamy, adoring, lovesick"goo-goo eyes"
About speech/soundsBaby-like, cooing, infantile"goo-goo voice/talk"

In one line: "goo-goo" describes either the helplessly adoring look of someone deeply infatuated, or the soft, babbling, infantile quality of baby-directed speech and sounds. Both uses suggest something sweet, unguarded, and a little silly.
6979: The word goo-goo as a noun has a small cluster of closely related meanings, plus one separate meaning from American political history. Here's everything you need to know.
Meaning 1: The sounds a baby makes

The most basic and widely understood meaning of goo-goo as a noun is the inarticulate, soft, cooing sounds that a very young baby makes — the kind of sounds an infant produces before they can form real words.

When a baby lies on their back and makes that bubbly, rounded, soft vocalization — "gooooo... gaaaa... gooooo" — that is called a goo-goo. These are the first sounds of communication a human being makes, even before babbling proper words.

Example: "She leaned over the crib and smiled at every little goo-goo the baby made."

Because of this association, the word also carries a broader feel of babyish or infantile behaviour. If an adult is being excessively silly, mushy, or childlike around someone they love (especially a romantic partner or a pet), people sometimes say they're "talking goo-goo" or behaving in a goo-goo way.

This is probably the most commonly used noun phrase built from this word. Goo-goo eyes refers to a soft, dreamy, adoring look that someone gives another person when they are infatuated or deeply in love with them.

Imagine someone staring at their crush with wide, melting, almost helpless eyes — lost in admiration, unable to look away, looking slightly dazed and smitten. That expression is goo-goo eyes.

The noun "goo-goo" here captures the idea that love makes people temporarily regress — their gaze becomes as soft and unfocused as a baby's, hence the connection to baby sounds.

Example: "He couldn't stop making goo-goo eyes at her across the dinner table."

The phrase is almost always used in the structure "making goo-goo eyes (at someone)." It has a light, gently teasing tone — people use it to poke fun at someone who is visibly lovestruck.
Meaning 3: A political reformer (historical American English)

This meaning is separate from the baby/love meanings and comes from American political history in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

In this context, a Goo-Goo (often written with capital letters) was a nickname — usually a mocking one — for a member of a "Good Government" reform movement. These were citizens and activists who campaigned against political corruption, especially the corrupt political machines that ran many American cities at the time (such as Tammany Hall in New York City).

The nickname "Goo-Goo" came from the first two syllables of "Good Government" — Goo-Goo is just a shortening of Go-Go-v-ment compressed further: Good Go- → Goo Goo. Politicians who benefited from corruption used this term to mock the reformers as naive, preachy, and unrealistic — basically calling them babies who didn't understand how the real world worked.

Example: "The machine politicians sneered at the Goo-Goos, saying they were dreamers who had never run a real campaign."

Today, this meaning is largely historical. You might encounter it when reading about American political history of that era, but you won't hear it used in everyday modern conversation.

Across its main noun uses, goo-goo always carries a sense of softness, innocence, and something slightly unserious — whether it's a baby's first sounds, the helpless look of someone in love, or (mockingly) a well-meaning idealist in politics. The word itself sounds round and soft on purpose; its sound mimics the feeling it describes.
